title: Shadow Mapping Algorithm
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Shadow mapping renders the scene from the light source into a depth map, then compares each fragment's depth in light space with the stored depth to decide whether it is shadowed.
short: A fragment behind the first surface seen by the light is in shadow.
long: A fragment behind the first surface seen by the light is in shadow. A bias term avoids shadow acne caused by depth precision errors; percentage-closer filtering softens shadow edges.
proof: A fragment farther from the light than the first surface recorded in the depth map lies behind an occluder and is therefore unlit by that light.
consequence: Shadow mapping is the dominant real-time shadow technique.

title: Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Screen-space ambient occlusion estimates how exposed each pixel is to ambient light by sampling nearby depth values. Darkening occluded regions approximates global illumination cheaply.
short: Nearby geometry darkens creases and contact regions.
long: Nearby geometry darkens creases and contact regions. The effect is view dependent and misses occluders outside the sampled screen neighbourhood.
proof: Nearby occluding geometry reduces the visible hemisphere for ambient light, so counting unoccluded samples gives a multiplicative approximation to ambient illumination.
consequence: SSAO adds perceptual depth cues at low rendering cost.

title: Marching Cubes for Isosurfaces
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Marching cubes extracts an isosurface from a scalar field by subdividing space into cubes and triangulating the portions of each cube where the field crosses a threshold.
short: Turn a scalar volume into a polygonal surface.
long: Turn a scalar volume into a polygonal surface. The eight corner signs select a configuration from a lookup table; ambiguous cases require careful disambiguation to avoid cracks.
proof: The corner values determine which edges cross the isolevel, and a fixed lookup table gives triangle connectivity consistent across neighbouring cubes.
consequence: Marching cubes is a standard method for visualising volumetric data.

title: Bresenham's Line-Drawing Algorithm
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Bresenham's line algorithm rasterises a straight line using integer arithmetic by maintaining an error term that decides when to step along the secondary axis.
short: Choose the nearest pixel at each step without floating point.
long: Choose the nearest pixel at each step without floating point. The error term is updated incrementally from the line slope, making the algorithm fast enough for early graphics hardware.
proof: The error tracks the deviation between the ideal line and the selected pixel centre, so updating it incrementally selects the closest pixel in each column.
consequence: The algorithm is a classic example of efficient incremental computation.

title: Cohen-Sutherland Line Clipping
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Cohen–Sutherland line clipping assigns each endpoint a four-bit outcode describing its position relative to a rectangular viewport and uses bitwise tests to accept, reject, or clip the segment.
short: Quickly reject obviously invisible lines and clip the rest.
long: Quickly reject obviously invisible lines and clip the rest. If both endpoints share an outside region the line is discarded; if both outcodes are zero it is accepted; otherwise it is split at a boundary and retested.
proof: A shared outside bit means both endpoints lie beyond the same boundary, so the whole segment is outside; repeated bisection at boundaries converges to the visible portion.
consequence: Outcodes give a cheap early reject in 2D clipping pipelines.

title: de Casteljau's Algorithm for Bezier Curves
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: de Casteljau's algorithm evaluates a Bézier curve by repeated linear interpolation between control points. The intermediate points also split the curve into two subcurves.
short: Repeated midpoint-style interpolation evaluates and subdivides a curve.
long: Repeated midpoint-style interpolation evaluates and subdivides a curve. The construction is numerically stable and forms the basis of adaptive curve subdivision.
proof: Repeated convex combinations implement the Bernstein polynomial form, so the final point equals the curve value at t and the intermediate polygons describe two subcurves.
consequence: The algorithm underlies curve rendering and CAD subdivision.

title: B-Splines and NURBS
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: B-spline curves are linear combinations of control points weighted by local polynomial basis functions. NURBS extend them with rational weights, allowing exact representation of conic sections.
short: Local basis functions give flexible, stable curve and surface modelling.
long: Local basis functions give flexible, stable curve and surface modelling. B-spline basis functions have local support and form a partition of unity, so moving one control point affects only a limited part of the curve.
proof: The basis functions' local support and partition of unity make the curve a local blend of control points; dividing weighted basis functions by their sum gives the rational extension.
consequence: NURBS are the standard geometry representation in computer-aided design.

title: Alpha Blending and Compositing
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Alpha blending combines a foreground colour with a background using an opacity value: the result is alpha times foreground plus one minus alpha times background, with premultiplied or straight alpha used consistently.
short: Opacity weights the foreground and background contributions.
long: Opacity weights the foreground and background contributions. Order matters for non-premultiplied blending with multiple transparent layers.
proof: Alpha encodes the fraction of pixel coverage by the foreground, so a convex combination of the two colours gives the observed composite.
consequence: Alpha compositing enables transparency, antialiasing, and layered image synthesis.

title: False Sharing between Cache Lines
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: False sharing occurs when threads on different cores modify distinct variables that happen to lie on the same cache line. Coherence invalidates the whole line, causing heavy traffic despite no logical sharing.
short: Coherence granularity can create contention between unrelated variables.
long: Coherence granularity can create contention between unrelated variables. Padding or aligning per-thread counters to cache-line boundaries removes the effect.
proof: Coherence operates at cache-line granularity, so a write by one core invalidates the line in other cores even if they access different offsets within it.
consequence: False sharing can dominate the cost of otherwise embarrassingly parallel code.

title: Memory Barriers and Fences
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Memory barriers restrict reordering of memory operations by the compiler or hardware across the barrier. Acquire and release barriers establish ordering guarantees between threads.
short: Fences constrain when memory operations may become visible to others.
long: Fences constrain when memory operations may become visible to others. A full fence orders all four combinations of loads and stores, while acquire and release fences order only relevant subsets.
proof: Hardware respects the barrier's ordering constraints, so later operations cannot be observed before an acquire and earlier operations cannot be observed after a release.
consequence: Correct lock-free algorithms depend on carefully placed barriers.

title: Race Conditions and Data Races
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one writes, and no synchronisation orders the accesses. Racy programs typically behave nondeterministically.
short: Unordered concurrent writes make outcomes timing dependent.
long: Unordered concurrent writes make outcomes timing dependent. Some languages declare data-race-free programs as the only ones with defined semantics.
proof: Without an ordering constraint either access may occur first, so the resulting values and subsequent control flow can depend on timing.
consequence: Eliminating data races is the first step to reliable parallel programming.

title: DRF-SC Guarantee for Data-Race-Free Programs
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A data-race-free program on relaxed hardware behaves as if its memory operations were executed in a sequentially consistent order consistent with program order.
short: Race-free code can be reasoned about as if memory were sequential.
long: Race-free code can be reasoned about as if memory were sequential. The guarantee depends on hardware or language memory models satisfying the DRF-SC condition and on correct use of synchronisation.
proof: Synchronisation operations order conflicting accesses, reducing all observable interleavings to a sequentially consistent order of the remaining operations.
consequence: Programmers can use simple sequential reasoning when synchronisation is correct.

title: Branch Target Buffers
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A branch target buffer caches destination addresses and prediction bits for recent branches so the front end can fetch along the predicted path before the branch resolves.
short: Remember where branches went last time to fetch ahead.
long: Remember where branches went last time to fetch ahead. Mispredictions squash wrongly fetched instructions and refill the buffer with the correct target.
proof: Branch behaviour shows locality, so recording previous targets lets the fetch unit continue without waiting; incorrect guesses are discarded at resolution.
consequence: Target prediction is essential for keeping deep pipelines busy.

title: Speculative Execution and Reorder Buffers
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Speculative execution lets instructions past unresolved branches run, with results held in a reorder buffer until proven correct. Misspeculated results are discarded rather than committed.
short: Execute ahead but keep results private until they are certain.
long: Execute ahead but keep results private until they are certain. Reorder buffers also support precise exceptions by committing results in program order.
proof: The reorder buffer keeps speculative values out of architectural state, so a misprediction can be handled by discarding them and restarting on the correct path.
consequence: Speculation extracts parallelism beyond basic blocks.

title: NUMA and Memory Locality
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: In non-uniform memory access systems a processor reaches its local memory faster than memory attached to other sockets. Placing threads near the data they use improves performance.
short: Memory access time depends on where the data lives.
long: Memory access time depends on where the data lives. NUMA-aware allocators and schedulers try to first-touch pages on the socket that will use them.
proof: Remote accesses traverse an interconnect adding latency and consuming bandwidth, so keeping computation near its data reduces access cost.
consequence: Ignoring NUMA placement can halve the performance of memory-bound servers.

title: TLB Shootdown on Context Switch
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: When page tables change, stale translation lookaside buffer entries in other cores must be invalidated. A shootdown interrupts those cores, which flush affected translations and acknowledge completion.
short: Broadcast invalidations so no core keeps an old mapping.
long: Broadcast invalidations so no core keeps an old mapping. Frequent shootdowns are a significant cost in systems with many cores and frequent memory-map changes.
proof: Without invalidation a core could translate using an obsolete mapping; waiting for acknowledgements ensures no stale entry remains when the operation completes.
consequence: Shootdown cost grows with core count, influencing page-table design and kernel scalability.

title: IOMMU and Device Address Translation
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: An input-output memory management unit translates device-visible addresses into physical addresses and enforces access permissions. It lets devices use virtual addresses and protects memory from faulty or malicious devices.
short: An MMU for DMA-capable devices.
long: An MMU for DMA-capable devices. IOMMUs also support device assignment to virtual machines by isolating each device's address space.
proof: The IOMMU applies a translation table to each DMA request and checks permissions, so devices reach only pages the operating system mapped for them.
consequence: IOMMUs enable safe direct device access and efficient virtualisation.

title: Metastability in Clock Domain Crossing
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A signal crossing between unrelated clock domains can violate setup or hold time and become metastable before settling. Synchronisers with two or more flip-flops reduce the probability of failure.
short: Give a changing signal enough time to settle before it is used.
long: Give a changing signal enough time to settle before it is used. Handshake synchronisers and FIFOs handle multi-bit crossings where simple two-flop synchronisers are insufficient.
proof: Metastability resolution is probabilistic with exponential decay in settling time, so adding a synchronisation stage multiplies the mean time between failures.
consequence: Clock-domain-crossing discipline is essential for reliable digital design.

title: Brent's Theorem on Parallel Time
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: A computation with work W and critical-path length S can be scheduled on p processors in time at most W/p plus S.
short: Time is bounded by ideal work splitting plus the critical path.
long: Time is bounded by ideal work splitting plus the critical path. The bound is tight up to constants for greedy schedulers and underlies work-span analysis.
proof: A greedy scheduler keeps all but one processor busy while the critical path advances, giving the additive bound on execution time.
consequence: Span, not only total work, determines achievable speedup.

title: Message Passing Interface Collectives
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: MPI collectives such as broadcast, reduce, scatter, and allreduce coordinate communication among a group of processes. Allreduce combines values from all ranks and delivers the result to every rank.
short: Group communication operations hide the details of multi-party exchange.
long: Group communication operations hide the details of multi-party exchange. Tree and butterfly algorithms implement collectives with logarithmic communication steps.
proof: Combining partial reductions in a communication tree gives every rank the same associative reduction result after logarithmically many rounds.
consequence: Collectives are heavily used in scientific computing and distributed training.

title: Work-Stealing Schedulers
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: In work stealing, each processor owns a deque of ready tasks and steals from another processor's deque only when it runs out of work. The scheme balances load with mostly local operations.
short: Work locally, steal only when idle.
long: Work locally, steal only when idle. Stealing from the opposite end of the deque reduces contention with the owner and tends to take larger subtrees.
proof: Local operations need little synchronisation, while stealing transfers work from busy to idle processors, improving balance without a central queue.
consequence: Work stealing is the standard scheduler in fork-join runtimes.

title: GPU Warp Divergence
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: A GPU executes threads of a warp in lockstep, so when they take different control-flow paths the hardware serialises the paths. Divergence can greatly reduce effective throughput.
short: Threads that disagree on a branch run in separate passes.
long: Threads that disagree on a branch run in separate passes. Predication can replace short divergent branches with masked instructions to avoid serialisation.
proof: All lanes share one instruction stream, so distinct outcomes are executed in separate passes with inactive lanes masked, summing their costs.
consequence: Branch-free or branch-uniform code is important for GPU performance.

title: Coalesced GPU Memory Access
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: GPU memory is most efficient when consecutive threads access consecutive addresses, allowing requests to merge into a few wide transactions. Strided access wastes bandwidth.
short: Contiguous accesses by a warp minimise memory transactions.
long: Contiguous accesses by a warp minimise memory transactions. Array-of-structures layouts can fragment accesses, whereas structure-of-arrays layouts often coalesce them.
proof: The memory subsystem groups neighbouring addresses into one transaction, so contiguous access by a warp serves all lanes with minimal requests.
consequence: Data layout is as important as arithmetic optimisation on GPUs.

title: Load Balancing Algorithms
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Load balancing distributes work across servers or processors so no single one is overloaded. Static schemes assign work in advance, while dynamic schemes react to observed load.
short: Spread requests so that no server becomes a bottleneck.
long: Spread requests so that no server becomes a bottleneck. Round-robin, least-connections, and consistent hashing are common choices with different assumptions about request costs.
proof: Sending new work to the least loaded server reduces the maximum imbalance; round robin balances only when requests have similar cost.
consequence: Good balancing improves latency and resource utilisation at scale.

title: Content Delivery Networks and Edge Caching
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: A content delivery network caches content at geographically distributed edge nodes so users fetch it from a nearby server. This reduces latency and origin bandwidth.
short: Move content close to users to shorten network paths.
long: Move content close to users to shorten network paths. Cache invalidation and request routing determine how much traffic the origin still sees.
proof: Serving from a nearby cache shortens the network path and avoids repeated long-haul transfers when the cached copy is fresh.
consequence: CDNs are essential to the performance and reliability of large web services.
